sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe cardiovascular structure and function.
- Describe lymphatic and immune function.
- Recognize common conditions of these systems.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the heart like a house with two upstairs rooms and two downstairs rooms. The two upstairs rooms (the atria) are where blood arrives first, before it moves downstairs to be pumped out.

### Question 2

The left side of the heart is the strong delivery truck that sends fresh, oxygen-rich blood out to every part of the body.

### Question 3

The left upstairs room (left atrium) is where fresh, oxygen-rich blood arrives back from the lungs.

### Question 4

Valves are like one-way doors in a hallway that only swing in one direction, so blood can't accidentally slide backward.

### Question 5

The myocardium is the heart's strong engine block — the thick muscle that squeezes with every beat.

### Question 6

The SA node is like the conductor of an orchestra, tapping the baton to start each beat that the rest of the heart follows.

### Question 7

The heart's electrical signal is like a relay race — the SA node starts it, the AV node pauses it, then the ventricles finish the lap.

### Question 8

The 'lub-dub' is the sound of doors (valves) snapping shut inside the heart, first the inner doors and then the outer doors.

### Question 9

The left ventricle is the body's strongest pump — it has to push blood up hills to the brain and all the way to the toes, so it needs the biggest muscle.

### Question 10

Picture blood riding a loop-de-loop: it enters the right side, zips to the lungs to grab oxygen, comes back to the left side, and then gets launched to the whole body.

### Question 11

The aorta is the biggest pipe leaving the heart — like the main highway out of a city that branches into smaller roads everywhere.

### Question 12

The heart is a hard-working engine that needs its own fuel line — the coronary arteries bring it the oxygen it needs to keep running.

### Question 13

Capillaries are like the tiny driveway where the delivery truck actually hands off its packages and picks up trash before driving away.

### Question 14

Arteries are the outgoing roads from the heart, and veins are the incoming roads back to it — like the 'away' and 'toward' lanes of the circulatory highway.

### Question 15

Veins are like a slow, low-pressure return road that needs little gates to stop blood from sliding backward when you stand up.

### Question 16

Blood is like a delivery truck that drops off oxygen at every house in the body, then drives back nearly empty to the lungs to reload with more oxygen.

### Question 17

Systemic circulation is the body-wide delivery loop — out to every neighborhood with fresh supplies and back with the empties.

### Question 18

The pulmonary veins are the rare 'veins' that carry fresh, oxygen-rich blood — they are the return lane from the lungs after a refill.

### Question 19

A DVT is like a traffic jam of blood cells stuck inside a deep leg vein, blocking the flow.

### Question 20

A DVT is dangerous because a piece of the clot can break off like a loose rock, travel to the lungs, and block the flow of blood there.

### Question 21

The pulmonary loop is a short trip to the lungs and back — drop off carbon dioxide, pick up oxygen, return home.

### Question 22

Plasma is the watery river that carries all the blood's passengers — the red cells, white cells, and platelets — plus nutrients and waste.

### Question 23

Red blood cells are the tiny red delivery vans packed with oxygen, and hemoglobin is the box inside each van that holds the oxygen.

### Question 24

Hemoglobin is like a magnet for oxygen — it grabs oxygen in the lungs, holds it while traveling, and lets it go exactly where the body needs it.

### Question 25

White blood cells are the body's security guards, patrolling for germs and calling in backup when an invader shows up.

### Question 26

Platelets are the body's quick patch kit — when a vessel gets a crack, they rush in and pile up to plug the hole.

### Question 27

Red bone marrow is the blood factory inside your bones, busy making new red cells, white cells, and platelets every day.

### Question 28

Hematocrit is like measuring how full the delivery fleet is — what fraction of your blood is packed with red oxygen vans.

### Question 29

Anemia is like having too few delivery vans on the road, so the body's tissues don't get enough oxygen and a person feels tired and weak.

### Question 30

When oxygen runs low, the kidneys send out a chemical 'order form' (EPO) telling the bone marrow to build more red blood cells.

### Question 31

The Rh factor is like a special flag that some red blood cells fly and others do not — having the flag makes you 'positive.'

### Question 32

Type O negative blood is like a plain, unlabeled package with no tags on it, so almost any receiver's immune system will accept it without alarm.

### Question 33

A CBC is like taking inventory of the blood's whole team — counting the red vans, the white guards, and the platelet patch kits.

### Question 34

Leukemia is when the blood factory starts making too many broken white blood cells that crowd out the healthy ones.

### Question 35

The lymph system is like the body's drainage and recycling network — it mops up extra fluid between cells and runs it through security checkpoints (lymph nodes) before returning it to the blood.

### Question 36

Lymph is the clear liquid that leaks out between cells and gets collected by the body's drainage pipes to be cleaned and returned.

### Question 37

Lymph nodes are like security checkpoints along the drainage pipes, where guards (immune cells) inspect the fluid for germs and fight them.

### Question 38

You can think of lymph nodes as security stations set up at major intersections like the neck, armpits, and groin.

### Question 39

The spleen is like a recycling center for old red blood cells — it takes them out of circulation, salvages useful parts, and helps spot germs in the blood.

### Question 40

The thymus is like a training academy where young immune cells learn to recognize the body's own cells and attack only real threats.

### Question 41

Tonsils are like the guards at the front gate of the throat, catching germs that try to sneak in through your mouth or nose.

### Question 42

After you eat, tiny straws in the intestine (lacteals) soak up the fat from your food and send it into the lymph pipes to be delivered to the blood.

### Question 43

Lymphedema is like a backed-up drain in a sink — when the lymph pipes are blocked, fluid pools and the area swells.

### Question 44

Lymphoma is cancer that starts in the lymph system's guard cells, sometimes showing up first as lumps in the neck, armpits, or groin.

### Question 45

Your skin is like a castle wall — it keeps most germs out before they can even get inside.

### Question 46

When a spot gets inflamed it turns red, feels hot, puffs up, and hurts — like the body sending extra blood and helpers to that spot to fight.

### Question 47

B cells are like factories that build custom keys (antibodies) to match a specific germ's lock.

### Question 48

Innate immunity is the fast, all-purpose guard that reacts right away, while adaptive immunity is the trained specialist that learns each germ's face and remembers it.

### Question 49

Macrophages are the cleanup crew that literally swallow germs and old cell parts whole to keep the body tidy and safe.

### Question 50

A vaccine is like a practice drill — the immune system meets a harmless copy of the germ, learns its face, and is ready to fight the real one.

### Question 51

A newborn borrows the mother's antibodies like borrowing a friend's umbrella — the protection is real but only lasts a short while.

### Question 52

During an allergy, the body releases histamine like a fire alarm, causing the itching, sneezing, and swelling that come with the reaction.

### Question 53

In autoimmune disease, the body's guards get confused and start attacking the castle's own workers instead of invaders.

### Question 54

HIV attacks the immune system's team captains, the helper T cells, so the rest of the defenders lose their direction and can't fight well.

### Question 55

T cells are the field commanders and the strike force — some give orders and others destroy cells that have been taken over by germs.

### Question 56

After you beat an illness, your body keeps a 'wanted poster' of that germ in its files, so next time it can react fast before you even get sick.

### Question 57

An allergy is when the body's alarm goes off for something harmless, like treating a speck of pollen as a serious intruder.

### Question 58

Anaphylaxis is the body's alarm going off so hard it can swell the throat shut and make blood pressure crash — a true emergency.

### Question 59

Trouble breathing and swelling right after a shot is a red-alert — you call for help immediately, because it can get worse very fast.

### Question 60

Systolic is the push when the heart squeezes, and diastolic is the resting pressure when the heart relaxes — like the high and low points of a water wave.

### Question 61

Blood pressure is always two numbers, like a fraction: the top number is the squeeze and the bottom number is the rest.

### Question 62

A healthy blood pressure is like calm water flowing through a pipe — around 120 over 80 or lower.

### Question 63

Counting the pulse is like checking how many times the heart knocks in a minute — between 60 and 100 knocks while resting is the usual, healthy range.

### Question 64

Each heartbeat sends a little wave of blood through the arteries, and feeling that wave at your wrist is like feeling the drumbeat of the heart.

### Question 65

High blood pressure is sneaky — it can quietly damage the body for years without the person feeling anything at all.

### Question 66

A pulse oximeter is a little clip that shines a light to see how much oxygen your red blood cells are carrying — like checking how full the delivery vans are.

### Question 67

Atherosclerosis is like rust and gunk building up inside a pipe, making the opening narrower so less blood can flow through.

### Question 68

A heart attack is when a fuel line to the heart gets blocked and part of the heart muscle starts to starve and die.

### Question 69

If someone's chest pain spreads to their arm or jaw and they feel sweaty and sick, you call for help right away — every minute matters.

### Question 70

FAST helps you remember stroke warning signs: check the Face, the Arm, and Speech, and remember that Time is critical.

### Question 71

A stroke is like a power outage in part of the brain — when blood can't reach the brain cells, they stop working.

### Question 72

Heart failure means the heart's pump has gotten weak, so fluid backs up and the person feels short of breath and tired.

### Question 73

An arrhythmia is when the heart's drummer loses the beat — it beats too fast, too slow, or in a wobbly pattern.

### Question 74

Blood thinners make the body's patch kit work slower, so a patient may bruise more easily from small bumps.

### Question 75

For someone with heart failure, sudden weight gain and puffy ankles can mean too much fluid is building up — the doctor needs to know right away.

### Question 76

A very high blood pressure with a bad headache and blurry vision is a big warning sign — the patient needs medical help right away.

### Question 77

Standard precautions mean treating every patient's blood like it might carry germs, so everyone stays protected all the time.

### Question 78

Bloodborne germs like hepatitis B can spread through blood, so healthcare workers wear gloves and follow safety steps to stay protected.

### Question 79

Washing hands is like turning off the germ highway — clean hands stop germs from catching a ride to the next person.

### Question 80

When someone has a high fever with shaking chills, a racing heart, and confusion, they need a doctor or the hospital right away — not a home remedy.

### Question 81

Asking about allergies is like checking the 'do not use' list before starting — it keeps patients safe from things that could hurt them.

### Question 82

If a patient is allergic to latex, staff make a clear note and use latex-free gloves and supplies to keep them safe.

### Question 83

A sign is something others can see or measure, like a fever; a symptom is something only the patient can feel, like a headache.
